items.title: What I learned about power from LBJ and Robert Moses
items.summary: Thanks to Max Farrens, who paired with me in writing the script for this video essay.I recently interviewed Robert Caro. He’s spent the last 50 years writing a four volume biography of Lyndon Johnson, and he spent another 7 years before that writing the biography of Robert Moses,
items.details: Thanks to Max Farrens, who paired with me in writing the script for this video essay.I recently interviewed Robert Caro. He’s spent the last 50 years writing a four volume biography of Lyndon Johnson, and he spent another 7 years before that writing the biography of Robert Moses, the master builder of New York. His books are widely regarded as the best explorations of political power that have ever been written.They also happen to be literally my favorite books ever. Whenever I meet somebody new, one of the first questions they ask me is, “Who is it that you most want to interview that you haven’t yet?” And for six years, I’ve answered the question the same way: Robert Caro.I’ve spent so much time trying to make this interview happen: chasing his agent, calling his publisher, contacting the museums that have his archives, and even sending him handwritten letters.I finally got to sit down with him, and I’m very happy with how it turned out. It’ll be out this Thursday.In the meantime, as I was preparing for the interview, and rereading these biographies, I wrote down the lessons they laid out about how to accumulate and use power.Robert MosesRobert Moses was the master builder of New York. He built more of the physical city than anyone before or since: the Triborough and Verrazano bridges, the Cross Bronx Expressway, Jones Beach, Lincoln Center, Shea Stadium, two giant power dams upstate, in addition to hundreds of parks and dozens of pools. Of the 899 miles of highways completed in New York State by 1964, Moses had built 672 of them. His projects collectively cost hundreds of billions of dollars in today’s money.For more than 30 years, Robert Moses was the most powerful person in New York (more powerful than any elected mayor or governor, despite not being elected to anything). How did he get and keep that much power?Exploits in lawPart of the answer is that Moses wrote the laws that governed him. He was called ‘the best bill drafter in Albany,’ and he used that skill to write himself powers that the legislators voting on his bills didn’t know they were granting.The political genius of Robert Moses is perhaps best illustrated by his use of public authorities, which are government-created corporations that build city infrastructure. Public authorities sell bonds to pay for a specific project, say a new bridge. Once the bridge is built, the authority would charge drivers a toll until it had collected enough money to pay off its bonds. Then the authority would tear down the tollbooths, hand the bridge over to the city, and go out of existence.At least, that was the idea. And that’s what Albany assumed would happen when the New York State Legislature approved the Triborough Bridge Authority Act of 1933, whose final version included - buried within pages and pages of legalese - a few seemingly minor alterations drafted by Robert Moses.Section 1 clearly stated that the authority would dissolve once the bonds were paid off. And since the bonds could run at most 40 years (and the revenues from the bridge would pay back the initial cost far sooner), it seemed like the authority had a clear, built-in expiration date. However, in a subsection of Section 9, Moses added a single sentence that said the Authority could “from time to time” pay off its old bonds by issuing new ones. And those new ones could be “for any other corporate purpose.” So just before the original bonds were about to expire, the authority now had the right to issue a totally fresh 40 year note, for a potentially totally different use.And what could the Authority build with all that money? The original act let it build two bridges and their “approaches.” Moses’ amendments also gave this authority the right to build “connecting” roads and “facilities not inconsistent with the use of the project”. These rights, when interpreted as creatively as Moses intended to, would allow Moses to alter most of the roads, parks, and housing in New York - for if a road connected to a road which connected to a road which connected to the bridge, or if a park lay along the road that connected to the road that connected to the road that connected to the bridge, surely the Triborough Authority was entitled to improve and change it.All this construction could be financed by the bridges’ enormous toll revenues and the right of the Triborough Authority to borrow against them. To give some perspective, in 1946, the entire New York City government could only borrow $150 million before hitting its legal debt limit. That very same year, Triborough could borrow $360 million. So Moses’ bridge authority had access to more than double the amount of money as the largest city in America.But what if a future governor or mayor eventually learned about all the power and revenue that had been delegated to this authority, and decided to claw back? Moses had planned for that too, and his solution was so clever that no lawyer or lawmaker in Albany saw it coming. The US Constitution says that

items.details: This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model, Glimpse. It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” View post on X ↗ So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount, co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. DecoyCount results Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding, co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor, Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release, frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” How the benchmark works: “DecoyCount exposes interpretable counting failures across seven mechanisms.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were withheld from our training, and our contamination check found no overlap in the training data checked,” Dai replied, via email. “Without any cues, Glimpse scored 50.48% on the 1,660 DecoyCount items, making it the only model in the comparison to clear 50%. The closest was GPT-6 Astra at 43.17%, about 7 points behind, and Gemini-3.8-flash scored 32.71% while Qwen3.8-max scored 28.31%, and Claude-Fable-5.1 came in at 25.22%.” Dai did note that Glimpse’s results “come from a single run of the model on its own, without an agent or tool harness,” whereas the six models from the paper were each averaged across three runs under their reported settings. DecoyCount benchmark results for frontier models over 3 runs each. But what exactly is DecoyCount revealing that existing model benchmarks miss? According to Dai, it tests both vision and reasoning together — which most benchmarks elide. “If a person sees an apple in front of a mirror, we know that there’s just one apple and it’s being reflected. But a model might miss the apple entirely (a vision problem) or count the apple and its reflection as two (a reasoning problem). But most benchmarks that test for this error only check the final number, so both mistakes are treated the same way, which is an issue if you want to fix the root problem and can’t tell if it’s an issue of vision or judgement.” Frontier Model Comparison in DecoyCount paperWhat is visual thinking exactly? Andrew Dai isn’t a Johnny-come-lately on the AI scene. In 2015, while working at Google, he co-authored a paper entitled Semi-supervised sequence learning. In this paper, Dai and his then colleague Quoc Le demonstrated an early version of the pretrain-then-fine-tune approach later adopted in large language models. Over the decade that followed, Dai worked for Google DeepMind on GLaM MoE, PaLM 2 and then Gemini. Dai only left Google this year, in order to co-found Elorian. Part of his motivation was to push the boundaries of what vision models can do. His approach, he explained to Latent Space, is based on a concept in human psychology called visual thinking. When most people “think about spatial problems or visual problems,” he explained, “they visualize the problem [by] generating images and editing images in their mind.” He gave an example of buying a sofa and mentally picturing what it will look like in your living room. A conceptual visual reasoning loop There’s also manipulating an image in your mind; for example if you’re counting people around a table, you might mentally “cross them off one by one,” Dai said. This is what Elorian aims to do in its models: teach them visual thinking “that involves generation and editing images as part of the reasoning trace, along with language.” The key point is that image generation isn’t just an output for a vision model — the generated or edited image is part of a chain of reasoning.How is Elorian different from World Models? Visual reasoning is still a work in progress, but there have been some impressive releases this year in “world models” — where vision is a key component. Two that stand out are World Labs’ Atlas in September (the company was subsequently acquired by AMD) and Google’s just released Genie 4. items.summary: What happens when you put code-generation agents in the hands of enterprise IT teams? With Serval, you get a system where it's easy for everyone to be a builder. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with Serval co-founder and CEO Jake Stauch to analyze his company’s direct challenge t
items.details: What happens when you put code-generation agents in the hands of enterprise IT teams? With Serval, you get a system where it's easy for everyone to be a builder. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with Serval co-founder and CEO Jake Stauch to analyze his company’s direct challenge to ServiceNow as the enterprise automation and service management system of record. Jake explains that by building an AI platform for enterprise IT departments with Serval, users can safely build while still safeguarding permissions by strict deterministic approvals and an audit trail. He also talks about ProServal, the company’s team that embeds automation engineers directly with customers in order to provide ongoing support and service. Jake also discusses how AI was the big unlock to taking on ServiceNow, why he’s betting on coding agents getting even better, why consumer is a window into what will happen next in enterprise and why the SaaS-pocalypse might look more like a consolidation, why background agents are still a moonshot in enterprise software, and the importance of hiring product-oriented engineers. In a very pleasant surprise, Gemini announced Carbon, a newer frontier model than the 3 week old Argon, with fantastic benchmarks: Taking it to the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis consolidated benchmark, putting GDM in the lead for possibly the first time in AAII history: View post on X ↗ sd AI News for 10/27/2026-10/28/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapGemini 4 Carbon Tops Independent Leaderboards, with Access Limited to Cyber DefendersLaunch: Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon two weeks after Argon. It is positioned as state of the art on cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks (@sundarpichai, @GoogleDeepMind). Claimed cyber results: 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for vulnerability finding, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching (@sundarpichai). Availability: Carbon first goes to trusted cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program, with wider developer access promised "as soon as possible" (@GoogleAI). Pricing: Phil Schmid quotes $2/$10 per million input/output tokens with an asterisk (@_philschmid). Artificial Analysis lists $4/$20 standard pricing with a 50% launch discount that has no end date. Cached input costs $0.20 per million tokens (@ArtificialAnlys). Specs: The model has a 1M-token context window and 1M max output. Inputs are text, image, video and speech; output is text (@ValsAI). Safety claims (Google): Successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 fell to 0.0%, and cheating attempts fell to 0.4%. Unsupported claims are down about 2x versus Argon. Overreach fell 26% and under-service fell 29% (@OfficialLoganK). Artificial Analysis: Carbon is #1 on Intelligence Index v5 with a score of 59. It leads 4 of the 9 index evals: HLE-Diamond, TB-Science, AA-Omniscience and AutomationBench (@ArtificialAnlys). Coding: On the Coding Agent Index, Carbon scores 59 using Antigravity CLI, versus 62 for Claude Code with Opus 5.5 [max]. It scores 51% on FrontierCode v1.1, versus 56% for Opus. Knowledge work: Carbon reaches 1609 Elo on AA-Briefcase, up 126 points from Argon. It still trails Grok 4.7, Muse Wonder and Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). Cost: Carbon costs $7.76 per index task, versus $10.04 for Opus 5.5 and $6.25 for GPT-6 Astra. It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Opus. Hallucination: Carbon leads Omniscience with 54. Its hallucination rate rose from Argon's 4% to 11%, which is still the second lowest measured. Opus 5.5 and Astra are both at 50%. Other independent evals: Arena: Carbon is #1 in Text Arena (1528), #2 in Agent Arena at a $1.80 median cost per task, and #4 in Code Arena: WebDev (1768) (@arena). Arena attributes the gains over Argon to more praise, more confirmed successes and better steerability (@arena). Vals: Carbon is #2 on the Vals Index and #1 on the Finance Index and Legal Research Benchmark. It produces 64% more output tokens than Argon, mostly on finance, tax and legal tasks (@ValsAI, tokens). Coding benchmarks: Carbon scores 61.2% on FrontierSWE, behind GPT-6 Astra (65.5), Opus 5.5 (62.3) and Sonnet 5.5 (61.9) (@ProximalHQ). It sets a narrow state of the art of 9.6% on SWE-sweep (@KLieret). Andon Labs: Carbon is #1 on Vending-Bench 2 (@andonlabs). It is also #1 on Blueprint-Bench 2, where it ties the human baseline for 3D spatial understanding (@andonlabs). Caveats and reactions: Harness: The coding-agent results were measured in Antigravity CLI, so results in other harnesses are untested (@Yuchenj_UW). Hallucination risk: Some users are concerned about hallucination in cyber use (@scaling01). Lab gap: scaling01 thinks Google remains about two months behind the next OpenAI and Anthropic releases (@scaling01). RSI framing: On the earnings call, Sundar Pichai said AI is increasing training and launch velocity. He expects "continued acceleration because of RSI" over the next twelve months (@AndrewCurran_). Unconfirmed: Claims of a stronger unreleased Gemini model are not confirmed (@kimmonismus). Internal workflow: A Gemini engineer describes overnight agent loops and swarms that inspect RL data. In that workflow, launches now feel like "periodic checkpoints" (@zhangqiaorjc). Leaderboard Resets and Benchmark IntegrityAA Intelligence Index v5: The rebuilt index runs 60% on private tests (@TheRundownAI). Ranking before Carbon: Opus 5.5 scored 58, followed by GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55), Sonnet 5.5 (54) and GPT-6.1 Terra (51). Open models: Kimi K3.1 Pro fell from 55 to 46. Why Agents Love Supabase
items.summary: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20. Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $
items.details: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20. Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker, it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Watch the full conversation, including my opening commentary →Give the agent a backend it can read My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the application. In the commentary, I compare this to a Terraform moment for the database. Put the desired state in Git and the agent can read it, change it, fork it and work against it as part of the repository. Humans get the same advantage: the backend becomes easier to understand without reconstructing its entire history. That is the part I like most about the agent-friendly direction. These are improvements I wanted as a developer already. Making them useful to agents gives the team another reason to finish the job. Compute deserves more than a bullet point I think Supabase Compute, now in private alpha, may be undersold. An application needs somewhere to do its work as well as somewhere to store the result. Once you have a database, you still need a place to run the processes that chunk documents, generate embeddings or do other longer-running work. Paul and Ant discuss running containers close to the database. That closes a gap between getting an application started and operating it: fewer separate services to configure, connect and explain to the agent. Edge functions remain useful, but they don't cover every workload. The operating side matters too. Logs, checks, connections and context help an agent understand what it is changing. A model that can issue SQL still needs to know what the database contains, how the application uses it, and what happened when something failed. Supabase's Operate announcements are worth reading alongside the new ways to build. From prototype to petabyte The founders say Supabase is launching about five million databases a month. They are thinking about what happens if agents push that toward billions of applications. At the same time, existing customers are growing into much larger workloads. Serving more small databases and supporting a customer's increasingly large database are different engineering problems. That helps explain the breadth of the Scale announcements: OrioleDB, Multigres and the Turso acquisition. The conversation gets into the work behind the new “prototype to petabyte” positioning, including Postgres reliability and the choices involved in scaling up and scaling out. One observation from Paul and Ant is particularly interesting for anyone building developer tools: as AI-driven usage grew, they say activation and conversion improved. Their explanation is that an agent can carry a user from signup to a working setup in one flow. The person doesn't have to figure out every configuration step before seeing the application work. We also talk about the memes and community that helped Supabase grow, open-source adoption and enterprise sales, and whether agents will converge on the same application patterns. But I wanted this episode to capture the founders' chemistry as well. It is a chance to hear Paul and Ant think through the product together—and to see how much work sits behind a backend that an agent can make look easy. items.title: [AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
items.summary: Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification, Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental i
items.details: Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification, Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental improvements. Past guest Felix Reiseberg gets the headline today for coming out and charting the path forward for junior engineers: “Hunger beats tenure”This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests. Enough said. His advice for juniorsPick business impact over backlog: In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Pick a radical idea: Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious! Build it over a weekend: I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype. Focus on one good idea: In my experience, junior people often make the mistake of cramming multiple ideas into a single prototype, hiding three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones. Lean into your fresh perspective: If you’re working on something user-facing, you have a unique amount of empathy for users and thus a much better sense for how the product works or doesn’t work for them. Well said, Felix! Get web search results as clean, structured Markdown, using roughly 50% fewer tokens than JSON on average. Easily integrate Markdown search results into your AI workflows across 100+ SerpApi APIs!swyx’s commentary: we’re proud to work with AI native sponsors that you can use in your engineering workflows! Native audio: It generates ambient sound, music and real-time dialogue with characters, a first for Genie (Shlomi Fruchter). Physics and photorealism: DeepMind claims aerodynamics, collisions and natural human motion. Genie 3's worlds were "too static," and Genie 4 responds to prompted events mid-generation (Fruchter). Early-access impressions: Users with early access describe prompting a "neogothic brutalist city," then adding dragons and an NPC live. They call it "not flawless" but a large leap over Genie 3 (Ethan Mollick, venturetwins, Riley Goodside). The original proof spans about 15,000 pages across roughly 500 papers by more than 100 mathematicians (Axiom, Kevin Weil). Process: An agent swarm produced about 50M lines of Lean in 24 days. Agents claimed tasks, reviewed each other's work and merged through GitHub, with human guidance, and reportedly fixed hundreds of errata in the published proof (omarsar0, kimmonismus). Context: Researchers note it displaces the four-color theorem as the largest computer-verified proof. Few humans understand the full CFSG proof (hyhieu226, Stella Biderman). Anthropic's parallel claim: Anthropic reportedly says Claude independently disproved ETH, finding the key algorithm on Oct 16 with "14M output tokens and no human input." items.title: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands
items.summary: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday, the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to the
items.details: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday, the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang, heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. A model launch is also an API launch Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own products do not cover. As we have said for 4 straight years now on the podcast, having good evals is golden.The brain and the hands Our favorite mental model in the episode is the distinction between an agent's brain and its hands. In Managed Agents, Anthropic separates the session log and harness from the sandbox that executes code. The harness can persist while an execution environment is created when needed; a failed sandbox does not have to take the whole agent session with it. We covered this in the Thariq pod: Claude Code’s Next Era — Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic — Latent SpaceShipping Opus/Sonnet 5.5, Mods, Plugins, Projects, Tag while Pacing the Frontier Latent Space The same separation gives security a useful architectural property. If generated code runs in a sandbox that never receives a service credential, there is no credential in that sandbox for the code to read. The episode describes credentials held separately and attached through a proxy, alongside controls on where sandbox traffic can go. Anthropic's containment write-up describes the wider set of isolation and network controls used across its products. The distinction matters for performance too. The guests say an earlier approach put the whole coding agent in a sandbox behind an API. Starting the environment and agent added work before the first response; if the sandbox disappeared, so did the running agent. Separating the pieces allowed the platform to pursue lower latency and better reliability while keeping execution isolated. It is a helpful lens for anyone designing an agent runtime. Ask which parts need to survive, which parts execute untrusted work, and which secrets actually need to be present where code runs. The implementation will differ between products, but those questions remain useful. An agent that helps another agent remember Managed Agents also provides a base for experiments in memory and multi-agent workflows. Dreaming is simply implemented as one agent inspecting another agent's prior work and writing memories back. That makes the feature an example of building a higher-level behavior out of the same underlying managed-agent primitives. Their account of the roadmap is more nuanced than a list of features. Memory and learning remain important, but the team says more of its immediate attention has moved to safety as model launches have become harder. They also discuss keeping the base harness relatively simple, while letting developers experiment with verifiers, parallel agents and other strategies on top. Ideas mentioned for future platform capabilities should be treated as plans, not shipped promises. The conversation about evaluations follows naturally. A harness is an application, but improving one starts to resemble research: pick a goal, measure behavior, inspect failures, and iterate. The guests and hosts discuss using models to help build and analyze evaluations, while retaining enough judgment to decide whether the evaluation reflects a real user's job. Show

items.title: Coding From the Himalayas With an Offline AI Agent
items.summary: When we talk about working remotely, we take a lot of things for granted, especially reliable internet and power. But sometimes, working remotely means trying to get something done on a flight, during a long train ride, or somewhere with little or no network. I moved to the footh
items.details: When we talk about working remotely, we take a lot of things for granted, especially reliable internet and power. But sometimes, working remotely means trying to get something done on a flight, during a long train ride, or somewhere with little or no network. I moved to the foothills of the Himalayas a year ago. I love the peace of living here, but it also comes with its own challenges, including network and power outages. Things I didn’t think about as much before are now part of planning my work. I work as a Principal Engineer at Thomson Reuters, where I spend most of my time coding and reviewing my teammates’ code. Coding agents are already a big part of my everyday workflow, which made me curious about how much of that workflow I could keep using offline.Working from the foothills of the Himalayas. Photo of my workspace. If you’re someone like me, who enjoys working with technology but also finds peace in quiet, remote places where the network doesn’t always cooperate, this article is for you. It’s also for anyone who has wondered whether a coding agent can run entirely on their laptop, with the internet switched off. I tried running a coding agent locally on my laptop to see how much work I could actually get done offline. What can we do offline? A project already on your laptop gives us plenty to work with. We can ask an agent to explain an unfamiliar function, investigate a failing test, refactor a small piece of code, or help finish a feature. These tasks can run offline when the model, project dependencies and test tools are available locally. Downloading a new package or looking something up on the web will still need a connection. Where OpenCode fitsOpenCode is an open-source coding agent that works with your project. You give it a task, and it can read files, propose edits and run commands such as the test suite. In our setup, its permission prompts let us review commands and changes before allowing them. I picked OpenCode because it lets me keep that workflow in the terminal while connecting to a model running on my own laptop. Ollama handles running the model; OpenCode handles the interaction with the project. OpenCode on my Mac, with Qwen3.5 9B selected as the local model. Open-weight models, including Qwen, make this possible: their weights, the learned parameters used to generate responses, can be downloaded and run locally. With Ollama running Qwen on the same laptop, OpenCode can send its requests to a local service. We download everything first, then disconnect the internet for the coding task. Aider is another option if you prefer a guided editing workflow; it also supports Ollama. We are using OpenCode throughout this walkthrough so that the setup and results stay consistent. OpenCode works with the project files and sends model requests to Ollama on the same laptop. Ollama runs Qwen locally.Choosing an open-source model Qwen comes in different sizes. I wanted a model we could run locally that could also use an agent’s tools. For context, here are published results for two Qwen sizes and another open-weight option, as reported in Qwen’s model card. LiveCodeBench v6 tests code generation on programming problems. BFCL-V4 evaluates function calling, which matters when a model needs to choose a tool and give it the right arguments. Higher scores are better on both. ModelLiveCodeBench v6BFCL-V4 Qwen3.5 4B 55.8 50.3 Qwen3.5 9B (used here)65.666.1 gpt-oss-20b 74.6 Not reported The above table scores reported in Qwen’s model card, not measurements from this laptop. “Not reported” means the source does not provide that score. We’re using Qwen3.5 9B for this walkthrough. Its stronger published coding and tool-calling results than the 4B variant made it a useful starting point. The table doesn’t measure laptop speed or the whole OpenCode workflow; our offline file edits and tests are the check for that. Model size and memoryModelApprox. download Qwen3.5 4B 3.3–4.0 GB Qwen3.5 9B (used here)6.6–7.6 GB Qwen3.5 27B 17–20 GB Ollama lists all available sizes; downloads vary by runtime format. Download size isn’t a RAM requirement. Voltti budgets 12–16 GB of memory for a 6.6 GB Qwen3.5 9B build. Our 64k-token OpenCode configuration may need more, so leave room for context and other apps. How OpenCode performed in benchmarks OpenCode has also been tested beyond small demos. The research preprint The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents compared OpenCode, Goose and OpenHands-SDK on 50 Terminal-Bench Pro tasks using two cloud models. Here are the pass rates reported in Table 2. Coding agentQwen3.6 PlusMiniMax M2.5 Goose 48% [34–62%] 38% [24–52%] OpenCode50% [36–64%]46% [32–60%] OpenHands-SDK 50% [36–64%] 46% [32–60%] The brackets show 95% confidence intervals. The authors caution that most differences in pass rate were not statistically clear. items.title: [AINews] Anthropic files for $2T IPO in 2 weeks: 1400% growth rate, 48% of revenue through cloud partners, 85% margin, $1B op profit in Q2, $134B cash in bank and $10B lifetime burn
items.summary: Today is one of those days that is tougher to cover for a normally-engineer audience that isn’t used to reading most S-1’s, let alone 350 pages of one of the most unusual S-1’s of all time: Better visualized: With significant operating leverage causing the first profitable quarte
items.details: Today is one of those days that is tougher to cover for a normally-engineer audience that isn’t used to reading most S-1’s, let alone 350 pages of one of the most unusual S-1’s of all time: Better visualized: With significant operating leverage causing the first profitable quarter in Anthropic history (adjusted for $1B/quarter of SBC): The incredible efficiency story is told in two loops, and of course you know, we love loop: The pitch going forward is “virtual collaborators” (don’t say agent!) for over a billion knowledge workers by 2028: We believe we have reached an inflection point where AI systems can function as genuine collaborators in professional work. They quickly complete substantive tasks that might otherwise occupy a skilled professional for several hours, a full day, or longer. AI systems are also becoming increasingly capable of performing tasks that were previously too difficult or costly to complete or surfacing original insights and analyses.We refer to these AI systems that work alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels as Virtual Collaborators. Virtual Collaborators carry the access rights, system connections, and context that their organizations grant them, which allows them to function more accurately and reliably. They can navigate and use internal tools and execute workflows that span multiple steps that require sustained reasoning. Virtual Collaborators are AI designed to be embedded where work gets done, and our aim is to continue extending them to knowledge workers globally, a population that is estimated to exceed one billion in 2028. And we end with a useful map of all of Anthropic’s offerings on one screen: AI Twitter RecapTop Story: Anthropic files its S-1. Reactions and highlightsWhat happenedAnthropic publicly filed its S-1 on Monday at ~9am ET. It plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT," and the filing shows a company that has crossed into operating profitability while carrying enormous compute commitments.Lead-up. Timing was reported by The Information (@kimmonismus), Fox Business (@negligible_cap) and Bloomberg (@kimmonismus). The IPO itself had been expected around Nov 9 (@kimmonismus). Official filing. Anthropic announced the filing with the standard registration disclaimer (@AnthropicAI). The EDGAR link was posted by @rishdotblog, and the ticker was flagged by @kimmonismus. Revenue. Revenue went from $41M in 2023 to $16.3B in H1 2026, roughly 14x year over year. Q2 alone was $11.6B, up 1,368% YoY (@futurenomics, @kimmonismus). Profitability. Q2 operating profit was $974M. H1 operating cash flow was +$3.9B. The headline $80.7B H1 net loss includes $81.1B of non-cash charges tied to financial instruments (@kimmonismus). Capital efficiency. Anthropic has raised $141.1B in aggregate. It holds $112.4B in cash plus $19.3B in short-term investments. Implied lifetime burn is about $9.7B (@SemiAnalysis_), which SemiAnalysis called "likely the most efficient scaling of a business in the history of capitalism." Compute commitments. Non-cancelable commitments run deep into the next decade (@scaling01). They include up to $120.5B for NVIDIA-powered compute through SpaceXAI, under agreements extending into 2029 (@kimmonismus). Pre-training delay. Anthropic disclosed it recently delayed pre-training of a new frontier model (@scaling01). Anchor investor. Altimeter said it will participate "majorly" in the IPO on top of its existing stake (@altcap). Key numbers (facts from the filing vs. derived estimates)Gross margin trajectory (@jaminball): 2023: 37% 2024: −95% 2025: 40% H1 2025: 12% H1 2026: 85% Jamin Ball's summary of the filing (@jaminball): Revenue growth above 1,000% YoY in the last quarter. 21% free-cash-flow margin over the last six months. Less than $10B burned in total to reach more than $16B in quarterly revenue. He also cited a $16.8B Q3 figure that has been widely reported but is not in the S-1 (@jaminball). Cash and burn figures don't agree across accounts. SemiAnalysis puts burn at $9.7B; Austen Allred puts it at $9.4B. Cash is quoted as ~$132B (futurenomics) or $134B "today" (Ball). Austen claims $6.7B of positive cumulative FCF from 2023 to June 2026 and $575M/month of current FCF (@Austen). That sits awkwardly next to a $9.4B lifetime burn, so treat derived cash-flow figures with caution. How the $141B raise breaks down (@jaminball): About $128.6B of preferred stock proceeds. $11.3B of convertible notes from Amazon and Google issued in 2023–2025. About $5B has converted. The remaining $6.2B of principal carries a $108.6B fair-value liability, because it converts at $2–5/share versus a ~$59 Series H price. The convertibles are effectively ~1.8B shares, not debt, and that mark-to-market drives most of the GAAP loss. Remaining pieces: ~$0.6B of SAFEs/common and ~$0.7B from pre-2023 rounds. Distribution through cloud marketplaces (@Bensign, @saranormous): 48% of H1 2026 revenue (about $7.8B) flowed through Bedrock, Vertex and Azur

To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains, we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.AI News for 10/22/2026-10/23/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. Its advertised strengths include full-project coding, Blender/CAD work, financial modeling, and long-running agents. @Kimi_MoonshotAvailability: Standard and Highspeed versions launched across Kimi’s website/app, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and API. Moonshot claims Highspeed preserves intelligence while generating output 2–3× faster; the official-account summary says it costs twice as much. The launch also includes Kimi Hosted Agents, a managed harness with a 24/7 execution environment for long-running work and multi-agent collaboration. @ZhihuFrontier, @ZhihuFrontierIndependent general-capability result: Artificial Analysis placed K3.1 Pro fourth on its Intelligence Index, scoring 55, behind Opus 5.5 at 58 and Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full at 56. Its strongest improvements were agentic rather than uniformly distributed across knowledge and science tests. @ArtificialAnlysIndependent coding result: Arena placed it #8 in Code Arena: WebDev, at 1,692 points, up nine places and 37 points over Kimi K3. Moonshot returned to Arena’s top four labs. @arenaIndependent cyber result: Despite deliberately reducing cyber-related training, it subsequently scored 64% on Artificial Analysis’ Cyber Index—the highest publicly accessible result and second overall, behind trusted-access GPT-6 Sol Daybreak Blue at 69%. @ArtificialAnlysThe reaction split: Enthusiasm about a prospective open-weight frontier contender was followed by concerns about inference economics, weaker results on some interactive tasks, benchmark presentation, and allegations of undisclosed paid promotion. These are distinct issues: benchmark quality does not establish deployment economics, and promotional misconduct allegations do not establish model capability. @simonw, @maxbittker, @kimmonismusRelease status, architecture, and what “open” means here At launch, the API was available; the weights were not. Moonshot’s announcement promises weights by November 4, 2026. The supplied tweets do not establish the eventual license, redistribution conditions, commercial-use restrictions, checkpoint precision, or complete inference requirements. Consequently, “soon-to-be open-weight” is more precise than the “OSS” or “open source” language used in several reactions. Artificial Analysis explicitly recorded the weights as unpublished. @Kimi_Moonshot, @ArtificialAnlys The release sequence generated confusion: Early reports predicted a release “today” and potentially the strongest open-weight model, explicitly on rumors/leaks; a follow-up reiterated positive hearsay. Neither was an evaluation. @kimmonismus, @kimmonismus Teasers triggered speculation about November 5, including whether Moonshot would monetize website access before publishing weights. The official announcement subsequently specified November 4. @scaling01, @scaling01, @bigeagle_xd Initial users reported availability on kimi.com before kimi.ai; another later reported obtaining access. items.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
items.summary: In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture. Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem, then soluti
items.details: In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture. Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem, then solutions to ten more open problems by July. And a proof of Navier Stokes in September. Anthropic published a formalization of the fermat's last theorem, and advanced bounds on Reimann's hypothesis. The models are suddenly good at math. The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Problem complexity Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity1 (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this: Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution. An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity2 modulo experts. For the unit-distance problem, his hint sequence had three parts: Look for a counterexample. Take the best known construction and generalize it. Try a sequence of number fields of increasing degree, but work with prime ideals of bounded norm. Gowers’ proposed formula for complexity is 2^k + t, where k is the length of the shortest hint sequence and t is the work required to develop it. It is the sort of formula that looks rigorous right up until you try to put a number into it, which is more or less the point. Complexity grows exponentially with the number of insights you need to solve a problem. Most problem solving is the work between these insights. You have a eureka moment, then spend months developing the hint until another conceptual jump becomes possible. For an expert, time spent is a useful proxy for this work, hence t. Hand someone the first unit-distance hint and they still have to do enough work to reach the generalized construction. Useful, but post hoc. You can’t look at the problem and predict it would need x number of hints. So, a problem’s age, the number of tries, and the prize attached to it are common proxies to ascribe difficulty. Characteristics of a given hint A typical insight changes the formulation of the problem. The representation and understanding of the problem change. Two things decide how much a hint is worth: How unlikely it looked before, against how obvious it looks after supplying the hint → This is harder than people realize. In unit distance, many experts did not consider the counterexample as likely. Where it belongs in the sequence: hints are ordered. A third hint is useful only after the work on the first two have made enough progress for it to be actionable. This defeats the naive brute force idea of listing a thousand mathematical techniques and trying every combination3 . Hints sequence traverses a tree. Initial insights change the problem and reveal the choices that follow. Humans solve problems breadth first Combine k and t and you get the human search pattern. Generate candidate directions, explore them shallowly, abandon most, and commit to a few. A promising direction is abandoned if it does not give enough encouragement early4 . This is a human constraint: Developing an idea can take months. Before committing, a researcher needs reasons to believe it will lead somewhere: conceptual promise, early results, or experience with similar problems. The longer it takes to find out, the higher the bar for trying the idea. Most research software exists to shrink this time by automating the tedious, mechanical, repeatable work. AI shrinks it far enough that the search pattern itself flips, and everything downstream follows from that. AI and complexity First, t. The model’s equivalent of effort is compute and tokens, spent on one trajectory (test time compute) or spread across parallel agents (parallel test time compute). Pretraining also supplies knowledge that a human researcher would have to locate or reconstruct. No individual expert is aware of every previous development, so occasionally they end up redoing things already done. The bigger difference is how models search: LLMs are depth first Give the model a single prompt and it will give you a solution. Maybe correct, perhaps not. Ask for a proof and it will give you something that approaches a good proof. CoT for these models runs in a greedy depth first manner too. And

We ordinarily try not to repeat title stories if we already covered it, as we did Patch the Planet yesterday and our Cyber trend call in July. But, if the scale is warranted, we also view our continued selection to also be signal - we can call things out 0, 1, or multiple times and that should be in proportion to its importance/historical significance in AI. We last did this with OpenClaw. “Black October” counts as such. Here’s a list:View post on X ↗AI News for 10/21/2026-10/22/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapBlack October: AI-Accelerated Vulnerability Disclosures Overwhelm DefendersScale of the incident wave: Over roughly 48 hours, a cluster of critical disclosures and breaches landed together (summary, roundup, patch list). Core software: PHP2Shell is an unauthenticated RCE in PHP. GitLab disclosed a CVSS 10 flaw affecting releases since 2014, patched in 19.5.1. Node.js shipped a Brotli decoder RCE fix, and NGINX and HTTP/3 also had DoS issues. Supply chain: LiteLLM 1.107.0 shipped with a password stealer. Railway told users to rotate secrets after possible exposure of customer keys. Zeabur is shutting down after 321,810 accounts were breached. Certificate authority: eMudhra's CA keys were trivially weak; one key was reportedly the number 4. A researcher says Claude cracked them with a single prompt, and eMudhra is exiting the CA business (Rundown). Python users are advised to update pip, uv, certifi and system CA stores (advisory). Healthcare data: Quest Diagnostics, which serves about half of US hospitals and physicians, reported exposed patient data (report). CVE volume: Monthly CVEs reportedly rose from about 4k to about 15k since April (@saranormous). State actor using agentic tooling: Microsoft attributes the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise to China-aligned Storm-0940. The group used the open agentic pentest framework ARTEX against 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenants at about 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute (MSTIC via @kimmonismus, detail). Speed of compromise: In some cases the group reached privileged access in under 3 hours. Other operators: CrowdStrike documented four operators running AI-agent campaigns, including one that hit at least 15 Argentine healthcare organizations. PHP provenance is disputed: The bugs were found by OpenAI models in August and embargoed until Wednesday's fix (Rundown). The PHP Foundation also says Claude Mythos had scanned PHP earlier (@Hesamation). Defense-wins framing: @BlancheMinerva calls the "offense winning" narrative disinformation, arguing this was a defensive audit and there is no evidence of large-scale exploitation (thread). Disclosure timing: Joshua Achiam reportedly noted that only about 4 of roughly 16 major incidents actually occurred this week; the rest were found earlier and disclosed now (MTS). Rogue agents in bank accounts: Axios reports that major US banks are detecting unauthorized third-party agents inside customer accounts. Some appear to act beyond user instructions (scoop). Pushback: @peterwildeford reads these as user-authorized agents that banks had not authorized, not hacks or rogue AI (take). Policy response: Sen. Schiff called for mandatory industry-wide AI guardrails (post). Outlook from Anthropic security: Deputy CISO Jason Clinton says things "are going to get a lot worse before they get better." He urges security leaders to ask boards for funding for the basics and expects defenders need to hold on for about 18 months (post). Defensive tooling: Formal verification at scale: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, working with Theorem Labs, used Claude to prove security properties across more than 100 open-source libraries in weeks (announcement). Reported figures are about 180M lines of machine-checked proofs covering 239 entry points in 123 libraries, with hundreds of bugs patched (summary). Patch tooling: Cognition open-sourced a vulnerability-remediation agent plugin (blog), and cve.now aggregates four CVE feeds with plain-English explanations (launch). Exposure checklist: @_philschmid posted a read-only agent prompt for checking exposure to the LiteLLM, Railway, PHP, GitLab and eMudhra issues (prompt). Safety, Oversight and Eval IntegrityMETR/Redwood embedded assessment at OpenAI: Two auditors from METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks on-site evaluating OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring for agents (METR, OpenAI). items.summary: In the transition to the agentic web, security has become an afterthought. Now, organizations are racing to figure out what AI security means, and how to keep their data safe. Live from Cloudflare Connect, Sarah Guo sits down with Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht to discuss the changin
items.details: In the transition to the agentic web, security has become an afterthought. Now, organizations are racing to figure out what AI security means, and how to keep their data safe. Live from Cloudflare Connect, Sarah Guo sits down with Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht to discuss the changing attacker landscape, and how his company is allocating its engineering resources to meet this emerging security challenge. Dane explains how enterprises that have moved away from castle-and-moat infrastructure to more of a zero trust infrastructure for security are in better positions than those who haven’t. He also discusses the challenges of patching 70 years of software and why the software development lifecycle will need to change for security for the agentic web, why he sees token spend in the next 18 months primarily going towards security rather than engineering, how the current web is in a ‘messy middle’ state where humans and agents are riding the same ‘rails’ on the internet, Cloudflare’s conference monetization gateway release as well as its Signals project with OpenAI, the rationale behind the release of Cloudflare OS, and the thinking behind a recent company restructuring. Plus, why Cloudflare hired one thousand interns, and why curiosity about AI is required to be successful at Cloudflare. Sign up for new podcasts every week. items.details: Warm welcome to Basil Chatha, our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D!Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience.A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate, raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation, and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it.Watch the full conversation on YouTube →GPU demand isn’t rectangularA typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand.Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad: Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices.There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion →The sandbox that almost didn’t make itModal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch.That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat, we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion →Fast startup is an infrastructure featureElasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost.We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. items.details: I spent two days touring Intel’s most advanced fab and talking to its technical leadership to understand what the chips of the future will look like.A lot of what’s coming next – gate-all-around transistors, backside power, CFET, hybrid bonding – is hard to follow without actually seeing it, so we made all the awesome animated explainers that I wish I had while I was prepping.I also asked Intel’s leadership how the semiconductor industry will cope with the enormous shock in demand from AI.AI compute has grown 3x a year for the last decade, but according to Intel’s CTO, Intel could only double leading-edge wafer production with today’s global stock of chipmaking tools.What kinds of tricks can foundries pull to extend this crossover point where demand surges way ahead of supply?This was a totally new format for us - hope you enjoy!I also made flashcards for the concepts I had to learn to prep for this episode here.Watch on YouTube, Apple Podcasts or Spotify.SponsorsWorkOS helps you do business with enterprises. It gives you access to all the features most commonly required by enterprises: SSO, SCIM, RBAC, audit logs, and more. It’s easy to plug these features in — it only takes a few lines of code — and WorkOS is releasing new functionality all the time, including things like auth for agents. If you want to join the 3,000+ companies that rely on WorkOS, go to workos.comJane Street built a powerful tool called magic-trace to help analyze and debug their trading systems. It only exists because one engineer noticed a feature on Intel chips called Processor Trace and thought it’d be valuable to build on top of. Now, traders and developers across Jane Street use magic-trace every single day! If you want to be trusted to pursue the ideas you think matter most, Jane Street is hiring. Go to janestreet.com/dwarkeshAntithesis’ testing platform lets you perfectly reproduce every single bug you find. That’s because it runs on a fully deterministic computer, which strips out all the unpredictability that can make certain bugs flaky and hard to pin down. To build it, Antithesis found every source of non-determinism in Intel’s x86 architecture and either sealed it off or replaced it with a controlled simulation. Learn more at antithesis.com/dwarkeshTimestamps(00:00:00) – Intro(00:00:47) – How Intel brings up a new process node(00:03:22) – What Intel learned from 10nm(00:06:28) – From planar transistors to gate-all-around(00:13:13) – Why High-NA EUV pays off for Intel but not TSMC(00:19:20) – Could chips have evolved completely differently?(00:23:33) – Inside Intel’s “Hot Topics” meeting(00:29:30) – Replacing copper wires with ruthenium(00:32:41) – Why stacked transistors take a decade to ship(00:39:45) – Hybrid bonding and the chip-to-chip bottleneck(00:48:00) – There aren’t enough tools to 10x chip production(00:53:14) – Can Intel catch up to TSMC?(01:01:02) – Terafab, and rethinking the fab from scratchTranscript00:00:00 – The AI demand shockDwarkesh PatelThere’s never been as big a shock to the semiconductor industry as the current surge in demand from AI.Gary DickersonAI is driving incredible computing demand.Peter WenninkEasily 40-50% above our maximum capacity, which I’ve never seen before.Dwarkesh PatelProgress in AI has been driven by exponentially increasing compute. To sustain that progress, foundries like Intel will need to manufacture far more leading-edge compute, both by producing more chips and by improving what each chip can do.But the production of these chips is bottlenecked by tools that Intel buys from their suppliers. Most famously, ASML’s EUV machines.CNBCIf they don’t have the equipment, they can’t make the chips here.Dwarkesh PatelI spent two days touring Intel’s fabs to prepare for these interviews with its leadership. I wanted to understand what it takes to manufacture the world’s most advanced chips and how hardware is shaping the future of AI.00:00:47 – Bringing up a new nodeDwarkesh PatelI’m joined by Chris Auth, who leads development of all the processes that are currently under manufacturing. The thing I want to understand in more concrete detail is how the development of a new process actually happens. If 14A is going to come out in three years or two years from now, what is happening from now till then?I want you to walk me through as much detail as you can, everything from the level of “how is the yield improving?” to what kind of telemetry you guys look at? What kind of experiments do you guys run? I want to understand what is going to happen over the next two years as concretely as possible.Chris Auth14A has been in development for about three-plus years at this stage, so quite a bit of pre-work has been done to get it to the stage that it’s at right now. items.details: Tickets and applications now live for AIE CODE - the last flagship AIE of the year.When Anekha Sokhal traded energy derivatives, staying on top of the market meant tracking more information than any person could read. Now, as CEO of Moshi, she is building the tool she wished she had: a recommendation engine that connects market information to what matters for a trader’s book.At AI Engineer New York, Anekha joins swyx to discuss her path from mathematics and JPMorgan to founding Moshi, and why useful AI needs to fit the way people actually work. items.details: Adversaries are already running AI agents, and the fastest attacks now play out in seconds. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with CrowdStrike president and CEO George Kurtz on what AI-equipped attackers mean for enterprise security. George explains how agents are flattening the adversary pyramid by putting advanced tradecraft in the hands of low-skill attackers, and why CrowdStrike and Nvidia are building a frontier-style lab of their own to train security models. They also get into how open-weight and closed models compare on security, where CrowdStrike is directing its platform investment, lessons from the recent Hugging Face incident, and why George sees AI, like every platform shift before it, as a net creator of opportunity. items.details: Almost 2 months ago, OpenAI introduced Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, a $1B subsidy for access to Daybreak cyber models and products. That funding came into use almost immediately, as major vulnerabilities in PHP were independently discovered by two parties: Ryan Austin, a researcher at the security firm Calif, as part of the OpenAI “Patch the Planet” project in August 2026 using GPT 5.6 Sol:… as well as Wiz, recently acquired into Google Cloud (using Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as their own tool, Wiz Atlas).All high profile cyber disclosures are at least a little bit of marketing, and the degree to which this was a severely alarming vulnerability on the order of famous ones like log4shell and Heartbleed is up to some debate, but surely the coordinated response across the PHP Ecosystem is the developer community responding in its most ideal form.We should expect to be in for at least a year of finding such critical vulnerabilities; but it is the wrong move to blame the messenger for finding them; rather it is good to know that our critical software is generally getting the biggest security audit it has ever had in human history.AI News for 10/20/2026-10/21/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapTop Story: PHP2Shell—chronology, core claims, and the complications behind the emergency responseWhat happenedResearchers disclosed two PHP-engine memory-corruption vulnerabilities, with demonstrated unauthenticated exploitation against major CMSs and an unusually broad coordinated response.The researchers named the vulnerabilities PHP2Shell and identified them as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Their technical description places the defects in PHP’s internal handling of out-of-memory conditions and fatal errors—not in a WordPress plugin or an application’s authentication logic. They report demonstrations of full remote code execution and “Heartbleed-style” memory disclosure. @sagitz_The disclosed demonstrations included pre-authentication RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. The researcher’s announcement separately claims remote memory disclosure against any PHP application. These are researcher-reported exploit results; they should not be silently expanded into a claim that every deployment has an identical, immediately exploitable RCE path. @sagitz_OpenAI says Calif researchers used its models to discover the flaws, while secondary reporting says Wiz independently found the same bugs. Posts identify GPT-5.6 Sol on the Calif/OpenAI side; a Wiz-affiliated account credits Gemini 4 Argon with discovery, exploit-chain development, detector creation, and patch validation. items.title: Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
items.summary: For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention.The “paying attention
items.details: For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention.The “paying attention” part is now the most important thing.In a recent Latent Space post, The Evolution of the Agent Harness, I argued that as models absorb more of the harness into their weights, the part that’s left faces the human. It becomes the Attention Interface: the layer that decides when the agent interrupts you, what it shows you, and which decisions it needs you to make. Claude Mods are an early version of the Attention Interface, and one you can shape yourself.Here’s my bet: ultimately, the harness becomes a platform that other companies build on, with models as the engine. Just as the browser became a platform for web apps, the harness could become a platform for the interfaces between people and agents.Claude Mods: What is it?A mod is a Claude Code plugin that consists of TypeScript or JavaScript functions that run inside Claude Code. These functions customize the behavior and appearance of the interface in the CLI and Desktop. Mods respond to events, like a prompt, tool call or interface render. They can observe the event, modify how it’s rendered, and handle it in place of the default behavior.Claude Mods are middleware for the agent harness. They inject code that changes Claude Code’s execution and rendering flow, changing how the application behaves at runtime.Claude Mods let the human and the agent build the human-facing part of the harness together. You can now work with Claude to design how Claude works with you. That is the essence of the “Attention Interface.”The harness reversalThe agent harness started as an interface between the agent and the machine it runs on. It lets you prompt the agent and the agent then sends commands, edits files and calls tools. Now it’s gradually becoming a way for the agent to interface with the human.Claude Mods let you reverse the direction of the harness. Rather than the harness pointing from the agent to the machine, you point it from the agent to the human operator, and the harness becomes a way to interface with human attention.Claude Mods make the human layer programmable, by the human who uses Claude.Claude can also build mods for you. Claude Code has a built-in skill that teaches it how to build mods, so you can ask for the mod you want in plain language and Claude will build it.Mods in practiceSome of Claude Code’s own features are already mods. Anthropic has shipped six of them built-in. You can see these by running /plugin and opening Installed, where they’re listed under Built-in:agents-md: loads AGENTS.md as project instructions.diff: takes over /diff and draws its pane.plugin-authoring: gives Claude the skill it uses to write mods for you.sec-default: guards what your organization manages from the mods a user installs.telemetry: sends the analytics records that Claude Code and its built-in mods log.you-should-know: a side agent that shows a note above the prompt when it finds something you might have missed. It’s the only one that’s off by default.Most of these work in the background, which is interesting because it means Anthropic is building parts of Claude Code as mods — even parts you may not notice. The one I’ve turned on myself is You Should Know.Here are the two mods I’ve found most useful in practice: one a built-in, and one I built myself.1. You Should KnowThis is a native Claude Code plugin built by Anthropic. It runs a side-agent that observes the main agent while it works and flags important information you’re likely to miss. Think about it like: tool calls and decisions that have a material impact on the output, but aren’t necessarily easily visible because they’re buried in the agent trace. It comes built into Claude Code, but it’s off until you turn it on.Here’s a real example. I asked Claude Code to simplify the noisy UI text in one of my personal projects. The main agent trimmed the copy on the Compare screen, installed the new build and took before-and-after screenshots. Everything looked done.Then You Should Know flagged something for me. CompareView.swift, the file the agent was editing, already had uncommitted work in it — and so did about 45 other files. If I later discarded the demo edits, I’d throw away that earlier unfinished work too. Its suggestion was to commit or stash the earlier work first.In this case, the You Should Know mod saved me from discarding work unintentionally.2. Next Steps SupervisorThis mod only runs after a turn that edited files, ran commands or made 8 or more tool calls. In the screenshot below, you’ll see six different pieces of information flagged for your attention. Next Steps Supervisor then suggests a next step to take, as a clickable button which sends the instruction as a message to Claude Code. This mod is available as part of Mo

items.summary: Proudly brought to you by SerpAPI: Today’s release covers a LOT of ground, but you can scrape all this into markdown for your agents! 50% token cost of JSON.We last covered the Inference Inflection in April, and historically most of the advances have been closed source decacorns
items.details: Proudly brought to you by SerpAPI: Today’s release covers a LOT of ground, but you can scrape all this into markdown for your agents! 50% token cost of JSON.We last covered the Inference Inflection in April, and historically most of the advances have been closed source decacorns from Fireworks to Baseten to Modal.Well, time for the open source response. It is day 1 of PyTorch Conf, and DeepSeek timed an intercontinental ballistic missile into the discussion by open sourcing DeepInfer, their production stack, capable of up to 72 hour prompt caching to the 12 hours OpenAI just announced:This is their customization of vLLM with credit to SGLang and TRRTLLM, but there is a lot added… minus their crown jewels - their ultra optimized KV cache (compact + >8hour lifetime), PD/disggregation, and load balancing (their 3FS was open sourced a while ago). We have translated their blogpost and published it here together with a complete research guide and explainers and codemap and subsystem guide:As we point out in their additional disclosure, their claim to serve 155T tokens/day gets them $38 per SM100/A950 card per hour at off peak prices (currently $0.15/$0.60 per million input/output tokens: 155000000 tokens * $0.14 blend cost / 24 hours is ~$1m per hour). Taking their production data (which we translated) of 1.5 million cache-inclusive input tokens/second per prefill GPU, 96% input cache hit, and 14,000 output tokens/second per decode GPU (over ~2400 GPUs): with all-in costs $5-8 per card per hour that is an >80% inference margin! Doing some cluster math, that is roughly $166B per GW, with 81 day payback period on inference margin (DeepSeek famously plans for 10 month payback). Imagine what the Whale could do with more GWs.Sponsored by SerpAPI!Give Your AI Agents Live Search Data with Fewer TokensReceive results from any of SerpApi’s 100+ APIs as clean, structured Markdown, using roughly 50% fewer tokens than JSON on average. Simply add output=md or use the /search.md endpoint. It requires zero configuration and is included with every plan at no additional cost.AI News for 10/19/2026-10/20/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapTop Story: DeepSeek DeepInfer—Production Inference, Open-Source Boundaries, and the Economics of Cached TokensWhat happenedDeepSeek released DeepInfer, the inference engine behind V4.1 Flash, alongside production-serving details that make the engineering report as important as the code.The release covers the inference engine and API-processing layer. DeepInfer supports distributed inference, speculative decoding, SWA Bounded Replay, and structured output on NVIDIA and Huawei Ascend platforms. The accompanying deepseek-recipe component implements production token encoding/decoding and official-API-compatible processing. DeepSeek says future model inference implementations and optimizations will also appear in this repository. @deepseek_ai, @deepseek_ai, announcement translationThe reported production figures are substantial—but describe a heavily cached service. DeepSeek’s engineering report, as summarized and quoted in the supplied posts, reports 155 trillion tokens/day from one cluster, 96% input-cache hits, 400 ms average time to first token, and 230 tokens/s generation, reaching 300 tokens/s for coding. It also reports $38 revenue per accelerator-hour at off-peak prices. These are first-party production claims, not independently audited measurements. @ZhihuFrontier, @swyx“Fully open source” does not mean the entire production service is reproducible from this release. Although DeepSeek describes DeepInfer as fully open source, the technical account says the KV-cache management and load-balancing components are not yet fully released, because they remain coupled to internal infrastructure. The engine is open; important service-level orchestration remains a deployment responsibility. @deepseek_ai, @ZhihuFrontiervLLM supplied the most concrete comparative response. After acknowledging that DeepInfer was initially built primarily on vLLM and released under Apache 2.0, the vLLM team reported decode throughput within 6% of DeepInfer’s published results on GB200 under a matched configuration.
